findings.antecedent: Surface features smaller than 30 µm
findings.quote: Moving over such a surface still produces vibrations that can be perceived. Therefore, movement is necessary to perceive the roughness of surfaces with features smaller than 30 µm. In this way, roughness down to a feature size of 9 µm can be perceived.

findings.antecedent: Touching a surface with a rigid probe vs. directly with fingers
key_citations: Klatzky RL, Lederman SJ, 1999
findings.quote: When a surface is touched using a rigid probe instead of directly with the fingers... the intensity of the perceived roughness is higher.

findings.antecedent: Physical roughness (sandpaper grit size)
key_citations: Stevens SS, Harris JR, 1962
findings.quote: when physical roughness is expressed as a sandpaper grit size, perceived roughness is related to physical roughness by a power function. The exponent of this power function lies around 1.5.

findings.antecedent: Prolonged exploration of a surface of a certain roughness (adaptation)
findings.consequent: Perceived roughness of a subsequent surface
findings.quote: Roughness perception is subject to adaptation processes. This means that after prolonged exploration of a surface of a certain roughness, the perceived roughness of a subsequent surface might be changed.

findings.antecedent: Adapting to vibration with a frequency of 100 Hz
findings.consequent: Sensitivity to vibrational component of roughness perception (fine textures)
key_citations: Hollins M, Bensmaïa SJ, Washburn S, 2001
findings.quote: The vibrational component of roughness perception, which is most important when perceiving fine textures, can be reduced in sensitivity by adapting to vibration with a frequency of 100 Hz.

findings.antecedent: Feeling a smooth texture just before a rough texture
findings.consequent: Perceived roughness of the rough texture
key_citations: Kahrimanovic M, Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2009
findings.quote: a texture that is felt just after a smooth texture has been felt, feels rougher than the same texture when it is felt after a rough texture has been felt.

findings.antecedent: Physical compliance (object's ability to deform)
key_citations: Harper R, Stevens SS, 1964
findings.quote: Similar to roughness perception, perceived compliance is related to physical compliance by a power law. However, for compliance perception, the exponent is less than 1, namely 0.8.

findings.antecedent: Surface deformation cue (in compliance perception)
key_citations: Srinivasan MA, LaMotte RH, 1995
Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2009
findings.quote: by far the most information is derived from the surface deformation cue, which is consistent with the findings of Srinivasan and LaMotte.

findings.antecedent: Difference in heat transfer rate
key_citations: Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2009
findings.quote: In general, differences in heat transfer rate of approximately 43% can be discriminated.

findings.antecedent: Skin stretch (cutaneous cues) in friction perception
key_citations: Provancher WR, Sylvester ND, 2009
findings.quote: When the authors introduced skin stretch, perceived friction increased significantly. This indicates the importance of this cutaneous cue for friction perception.

findings.antecedent: Physical viscosity
key_citations: Stevens SS, Guirao M, 1964
findings.quote: a power law was found relating physical to perceived viscosity, with an exponent of 0.43. This means that perceived viscosity ‘levels off' with increasing physical viscosity.

findings.antecedent: Lower viscosities (thinner liquids)
key_citations: Bergmann Tiest WM, Vrijling ACL, Kappers AML, 2013
findings.quote: For lower viscosities (thinner liquids), this fraction increased up to 100% for liquids as thin as water, meaning that it is relatively harder to distinguish thinner liquids from each other than thicker liquids.

findings.antecedent: Inertial force alone (for weight perception)
findings.consequent: Perceived heaviness compared to gravitational force
key_citations: Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2010
findings.quote: heaviness based on this inertial force alone is perceived as half of that based on gravitational force alone.

findings.antecedent: Smaller contact area (object lying on hand)
key_citations: Bergmann Tiest WM, Lyklema C, Kappers AML, 2012
findings.quote: the perceived weight of an object lying on the hand depends on the contact area: the smaller the contact area, the larger the perceived weight.

findings.antecedent: Smaller object of equal weight compared to a larger one
key_citations: Ellis RR, Lederman SJ, 1993
findings.quote: This might be related to the well-known size-weight illusion, in which a smaller object of equal weight is perceived as heavier than a larger one.

findings.antecedent: Increasing curvedness of stimuli (elliptic and hyperbolic paraboloids)
key_citations: Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, Lichtenegger I, 1994
findings.quote: Increasing the curvedness, increased the number of correct classifications.

findings.antecedent: Blind observers (early and late blind, not congenitally blind) vs. blindfolded sighted observers
findings.consequent: Performance in haptic discrimination of 3D shapes
key_citations: Norman JF, Bartholomew AN, 2011
findings.quote: blind observers (early and late blind, but not congenitally blind) performed better in a haptic discrimination with these 3D shapes than blindfolded observers.

findings.antecedent: Overall gradient of the stimulus (curvature perception)
key_citations: Gordon IA, Morison V, 1982
findings.quote: the overall gradient of the stimulus determines the curvature discrimination threshold.

findings.antecedent: Height information only (zeroth order) vs. slope information (first order) in curvature stimuli
key_citations: Pont SC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1999
findings.quote: performance with the stimuli that just contained height information was much worse than with those that also contained slope information.

findings.antecedent: Palmar side vs. dorsal side of the hand (for curvature discrimination)
key_citations: Pont SC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1997
findings.quote: Performance with the palmar side was significantly better, indicating again that cutaneous receptors play an essential role in curvature discrimination, as the density of these receptors is much lower on the dorsal side of the hand.

findings.antecedent: Increasing length of stimuli (curved strips)
key_citations: Pont SC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1999
findings.quote: Increasing the length of the stimuli not only causes a decrease of the curvature discrimination threshold, but it also increases the perceived curvature of the stimulus.

findings.antecedent: Length of hand (longer than wide)
findings.consequent: Perceived curvature of a spherical object
key_citations: Pont SC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1998
findings.quote: since most hands are longer than wide (see Figure 6), a spherical object would not feel spherical but ellipsoidal.

findings.antecedent: First order information (slope) vs. just height information (zeroth order) in dynamic touch
key_citations: Wijntjes MWA, Sato A, Hayward V, Kappers AML, 2009
findings.quote: They showed that curvature discrimination thresholds were the same as soon as first order information was available; stimuli containing just height information led to much higher discrimination thresholds.

findings.antecedent: Finger-span method vs. moving a finger/hand over the object (for length perception)
key_citations: Jastrow J, 1886
findings.quote: This latter method is less accurate than the finger-span method.

findings.antecedent: Wider glasses vs. taller glasses (same actual volume)
key_citations: Krishna A, 2006
findings.quote: She found that wider glasses were estimated to have a larger volume than taller glasses, even though their actual volume was the same.

findings.antecedent: Sphere vs. tetrahedron vs. cube (for same perceived volume)
key_citations: Kahrimanovic M, Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2010
findings.quote: for objects to be perceived as having the same volume, a sphere has to be more than 60% larger than that of a tetrahedron and about 30% larger than that of a cube.

findings.antecedent: Surface area of objects
key_citations: Kahrimanovic M, Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2010
findings.quote: participants (unconsciously) used surface area instead of volume to perform this task.

findings.antecedent: Wire frame stimuli vs. solid stimuli (for volume discrimination)
key_citations: Kahrimanovic M, Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2010
findings.quote: Volume discrimination experiments with the wire frame stimuli led to even larger biases than with the solid stimuli.

findings.antecedent: Time delay between touching reference and test bars (parallelity task)
key_citations: Zuidhoek S, Kappers AML, van der Lubbe RHJ, Postma A, 2003
findings.quote: a delay between touching the reference and test bars counterintuitively reduces the deviations.

findings.antecedent: Non-informative vision (allowed to look around room without seeing stimuli)
key_citations: Newport R, Rabb B, Jackson SR, 2002
Zuidhoek S, Visser A, Bredero ME, Postma A, 2004
findings.quote: when participants are not blindfolded, but are allowed to look around in the experimentation room (without seeing the stimuli), their performance improves.

findings.antecedent: Prescribed hand orientation (egocentric reference frame)
key_citations: Kappers AML, Viergever RF, 2006
Kappers AML, Liefers BJ, 2012
findings.quote: when participants are requested to hold their hands in a prescribed orientation, the deviations clearly change with hand orientation.

findings.antecedent: Cardinal orientations (horizontal/vertical) vs. oblique orientations
key_citations: Lechelt EC, Verenka A, 1980
Appelle S, Countryman M, 1986
findings.quote: performance is better with cardinal (i.e. horizontal and vertical) orientations than with oblique orientations.

findings.antecedent: Small number of items (up to three)
findings.consequent: Speed and accuracy of numerosity judgment
key_citations: Riggs KJ, Ferrand L, Lancelin D, Fryziel L, Dumur G, Simpson A, 2006
Plaisier MA, Bergmann Tiest WM, Kappers AML, 2009
findings.quote: For larger numbers of items (above three or four), observers are slower and more error-prone. This phenomenon has mostly been studied in vision, but recently a few studies were published showing that subitizing also occurs in touch.

findings.antecedent: Explicit instruction to use body-centered reference cues (Müller-Lyer illusion)
key_citations: Millar S, Al-Attar Z, 2002
findings.quote: it was shown that both in vision and in haptics the illusion could be reduced to almost zero, if observers were explicitly instructed to use body-centered reference cues.

findings.antecedent: Running fingers along a curved edge (adaptation)
findings.consequent: Perceived curvature of a subsequent straight edge
key_citations: Gibson JJ, 1933
findings.quote: Most of them commented that the straight edge felt curved in a direction opposite to that of the adaptation curvature.

findings.antecedent: Adaptation period of 2 seconds (curvature after-effect)
key_citations: Vogels IMLC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1996
findings.quote: an adaptation period of 2 seconds was already sufficient to give rise to significant after-effects and after 10 seconds of adaptation, the phenomenal flatness reaches a saturation level, so the build-up of the after-effect is quite fast.

findings.antecedent: Delay of 40 seconds or more after touching adaptation curvature (curvature after-effect)
key_citations: Vogels IMLC, Kappers AML, Koenderink JJ, 1997
findings.quote: Even after a delay of 40 seconds or more after touching the adaptation curvature, a significant after-effect could be measured.

findings.antecedent: Active exploration with index finger (curvature after-effect)
findings.consequent: Transfer of after-effect to other hand
key_citations: van der Horst BJ, Willebrands WP, Kappers AML, 2008
findings.quote: if a curved surface is actively explored with the index finger, the after-effect also transfers to the other hand.

findings.antecedent: Alternating warm and cold bars (thermal grill illusion)
key_citations: Craig AD, Bushnell MC, 1994
findings.quote: not an average or intermediate temperature is perceived, but a rather painful sensation of strong heat.

findings.antecedent: Number of brief pulses at three different locations (cutaneous rabbit illusion)
key_citations: Geldard FA, Sherrick CE, 1972
findings.quote: these pulses could be perceived as uniformly distributed between the two extreme locations... perceived as a smooth progression of taps on the arm.

findings.antecedent: Haptically augmented progress and scroll bars on GUI touchscreens
key_citations: Leung R, MacLean K, Bue Bertelsen M, Saubhasik M, 2007
findings.quote: haptically augmented progress and scroll bars on GUI touchscreens led to a significant improvement in terms of time to complete a task.

findings.antecedent: Haptic feedback in remote devices (e.g., telesurgery)
findings.quote: The fact that haptic information is lacking is considered a problem that should be solved in order to improve performance with such remote devices or at least make the use of them more intuitive.

findings.antecedent: Haptic feedback (beyond force/vibrations) in virtual reality
findings.quote: For the benefit of increased realism, haptic feedback that goes beyond just force feedback or vibrations is desirable.
